claims.text: Increasing Al and/or Cr concentration in multiprincipal-element alloys promotes formation of a continuous oxide scale.
The oxide scale promoted by increased Al and/or Cr is self-healing.
A continuous, self-healing oxide scale limits oxygen diffusion into the alloy.
Limiting oxygen diffusion through the scale governs oxidation resistance and material integrity during sustained high-temperature exposure.
The baseline alloy naturally forms a less protective and possibly discontinuous oxide scale during high-temperature oxidation.
The protective scale is primarily composed of Al2O3 and/or Cr2O3.
Higher concentrations of oxidation-active elements cause those elements to diffuse to the alloy surface.
Al and/or Cr preferentially oxidize at the surface.
Preferential oxidation of Al and/or Cr forms an effective barrier to further oxygen ingress.
Lower reactive-element content produces non-uniform or discontinuous oxide scales.
Non-uniform or discontinuous oxide scales permit faster oxidation and degradation.
The modified alloy will form a thinner oxide scale than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will form a more uniform and adherent oxide scale than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will exhibit lower oxygen uptake or oxidation-associated mass gain than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will retain microstructural integrity better than the baseline alloy after oxidation.
The modified alloy will retain mechanical properties better than the baseline alloy after oxidation.
The proposed mechanism is anticipated to operate during sustained oxidation in oxygen-rich environments from approximately 700°C to 1200°C.
The threshold Al and/or Cr content required for continuous oxide formation varies with the alloy system.
